study.title: Prefill and decode with the KV-cache

focus: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and writes one key-value pair per prompt token per layer; decode reads the full cache back for each new token and appends one pair.
TTFT covers scheduling delay plus prompt processing; per-token latency covers one decode step. Offline batch work cares about tokens per second, chat cares about both.
The manifest entries that move every estimate are layer count, hidden size, head counts with key-value heads, prompt and output lengths, batch size and precision.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the request path for the invented 64-layer model in the inference chapter's Worked Problems (D=4096, F=16384, N=32, K=8, H=256): total parameters 18.4e9, int8 key-value bytes per token 262,144, and the per-layer append of one [K, H] key plus one [K, H] value per new token. Derive both numbers from the manifest.
traps: Treating prefill and decode as one regime. Prefill is a batched parallel pass; decode is serial with cache reads, so one batch size or one roofline cannot cover both.
Counting tokens without naming prefill versus output tokens. Cost, latency and cache all scale with the two lengths differently.
Assuming batching speeds up every part. Batching reuses weights across requests, but each request adds its own key-value reads.

selfTest.q: A 512-token prompt arrives. What does prefill produce, and what does each decode step then read and write?
selfTest.a: Prefill processes all 512 tokens in parallel, writes 512 key-value pairs per layer and returns first-token logits. Each decode step reads the full cache, samples one token, and appends its pair.

selfTest.q: Which manifest entries must a shape manifest contain for this section's estimates?
selfTest.a: Layer count, hidden size, feed-forward size, query and key-value head counts with head dimension, prompt and output lengths, batch size, precision, and later the sharding.

selfTest.q: Why does batching raise linear-layer efficiency but not remove the decode bottleneck?
selfTest.a: Batching reuses each weight across requests, but every request adds its own key-value bytes, so cache traffic grows with batch while weight traffic does not.

selfTest.q: Which latency does a longer prompt directly worsen, TTFT or per-token latency?
selfTest.a: TTFT, through prompt processing time. Per-token latency is set by one decode step over weights plus cache.

study.title: Dense walk: 2P operations per token
study.locator: flops counting, with the How many flops in a matmul? box in kv cache
study.depth: The attention scale is 1 over the square root of head dimension on the live page; if your copy renders it without the root, trust the root. The 2P rule is decode-only.

study.title: Key-value cache FLOP savings grow with sequence
study.locator: kv cache: the one-sixth saving paragraph and the no-cache quadratic paragraph

focus: One matmul through all parameters costs \(2P\) operations by the \(2mnp\) rule; the layer walk (qkv, output, MLP) sums to the same within 2%.
Decode attention per token scales with cached length (\(4SN_{\text{heads}}H\) per layer for scores plus values); prefill attention scales with prompt length squared.

Softmax, norms, sampling and the unembedding are \(O(d_{\text{model}})\) per layer against \(O(d_{\text{model}}^2)\) dense work; they matter only when the dense term shrinks or a profile says otherwise.
Use head count times head dimension, not model width, wherever key-value heads differ from query heads.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive decode operations per token for the invented 18.4e9-parameter model at cached length 8192: dense \(2 \times 18.4 \times 10^9 = 3.68 \times 10^{10}\), attention \(4 \times 8192 \times 32 \times 256 \times 64 = 1.72 \times 10^{10}\), total about \(5.4 \times 10^{10}\).
traps: Applying 2P to prefill. Prefill pays the dense term per prompt token plus quadratic attention; 2P per token describes one decode step.
Writing the attention scale as division by head dimension. The implemented scale is \(1/\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}\); the count is unchanged but a kernel you write later must use the root.
Calling attention free in decode because 2P dominates. At 8192 cached tokens the invented model's attention is nearly half the dense count; recompute the share before dropping it.

selfTest.q: How many dense operations does one decode step take for the invented 18.4e9-parameter model?
At cached length 8192, what is its decode attention count, and what share is that?
selfTest.a: \(4 \times 8192 \times 32 \times 256 \times 64 = 1.72 \times 10^{10}\), nearly half the dense count, so it cannot be dropped there.
It counts one token through stationary weights. Prefill runs all prompt tokens at once with quadratic attention, and sampling plus unembedding add their own terms.

selfTest.q: Without a cache, how does per-step work grow with sequence length n?
selfTest.a: Each step recomputes keys and values for all n tokens: \(2 \times 2 \times n \times L \times d^2\) operations, or n/6 of a full pass, so totals grow quadratically.

units.title: Parameter, activation, workspace and KV-cache memory
outcomes: Derive parameter bytes under storage versus execution precision for a named model.
Derive key-value bytes per token and per request for MHA, GQA and MQA from layer, head and precision entries.
Fit a batch under a capacity bound with an explicit overhead line, and name what the fit ignores (activations, workspace, allocator).
units.why: Memory decides the maximum batch before any timing starts. A fit that forgets precision, head grouping or allocator overhead fails at load time, not at arithmetic time.

study.title: LLaMA-2-13B bytes: parameters, activations, key-value cache
study.locator: What about memory? and Modeling throughput and latency for LLaMA 2-13B, including the parameter table and both batch tables
study.depth: The tables label memory GiB but divide decimal gigabytes by bytes per second (32.7e9 bytes at 6.56e12 bytes/s gives 4.98 ms). Recompute in bytes and keep GB apart from GiB.

study.title: Weights, key-value bytes per token and the capacity fit
study.locator: kv cache: the bytes-per-token formula; capacity
study.depth: Recompute both byte lines: 52e9 parameters at 2 bytes is 104e9 bytes (about 104 GB), and exact key-value bytes per token are 2,097,152. The article's rounded 0.002 GB per token gives about 28000 tokens on 4 GPUs, not the printed 23000; use your own number with a stated overhead.

study.title: Intermediate and workspace bytes
study.locator: intermediate memory costs: tensor contractions, statistical normalizations and element-wise operators, with GPU Kernel Fusion

focus: Parameters cost bytes-per-value times count under the stored precision; execution precision can differ (int8 weights with bf16 compute) and changes later intensities, not this line.

Key-value bytes per token are \(2 \times \text{bytes} \times L \times K \times H\); the \(4 \times L \times d_{\text{model}}\) shortcut assumes key-value width equals model width and breaks under GQA and MQA.
Activations are megabytes where the cache is gigabytes at 8k context (80 MB against 6.7 GB in the 13B example), but they still set the workspace and fragmentation overhead you must state.
Capacity fits subtract weights first, then divide by per-request cache; always add an overhead line for allocator, workspace and graphs instead of absorbing it into rounding.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the 13B bf16 cache at 8192 context (\(2 \times 2 \times 128 \times 40 \times 40 \times 8192 = 6.7 \times 10^9\) bytes), then the GQA variant with 8 key-value heads in int8 (81,920 bytes per token), then fit 8192-length requests beside 26 GB of weights on 8 16 GB cards (about 150).
traps: Reading the inference chapter's tables as GiB. The step times divide decimal gigabytes by bytes per second; recompute in bytes and keep GB apart from GiB.

Copying the article's 23000-token fit. Its own rounded 0.002 GB per token gives about 28000 (about 26700 with exact bytes); the printed 23000 carries an unstated discount, so publish your own overhead instead.
Calling activations negligible everywhere. They are negligible beside an 8k cache; at short context with large batch they set the workspace line.

selfTest.q: How many key-value bytes per token does the invented model (L=64, K=32, H=256) use in bf16?
selfTest.a: \(2 \times 2 \times 64 \times 32 \times 256 = 2{,}097{,}152\) bytes (2 MB); with K=8 in int8 it is 262,144 bytes.

selfTest.q: How many per token for a 40-layer, 8 key-value head, 128-dim model in int8?
Three 40 GB cards hold the 52B weights (104 GB). Can they serve batch 4 at 2048 tokens each?
selfTest.a: No. 16 GB remain, fitting about 7600 tokens against 8192 needed. Serve batch 3, shorten context, add a card, or shrink the cache.

selfTest.q: When does the per-token shortcut 4 x layers x model width fail?
selfTest.a: Whenever key-value width differs from model width: GQA and MQA need the explicit K and H entries.
